paragraphs: R. Yeshavav the scribe divided all his possessions among the poor. Rabban Gamliel the Elder sent him word, 'Did they not say: a fifth of one's possessions for a commandment?' (See his entry.) In בש״ר [possibly Zayit Ra’anan on Yalkut Shimoni], beginning of Pekudei, he writes: It implies that he lived in Rabban Gamliel the Elder's time. Yet in the second chapter of Ḥullin, mishnah 4 (32a), R. Yeshavav said to R. Akiva, etc., and R. Akiva returned to R. Yeshavav's words. In Nazir (65a): a case involving R. Yeshavav, etc.; R. Akiva said to him, 'All your labor was in vain.' In Ḥullin (30b), R. Yeshavav says, etc., R. Akiva says, etc. In Arakhin (28a) and Ketubbot (50, beginning of side a), R. Akiva did not allow him to give away all his possessions. In Ketubbot (29b), he said, 'Let us cry out against Akiva ben Yosef,' etc. This implies that he lived in R. Akiva's time, which was after the destruction; thus it implies that R. Yeshavav did not live in Rabban Gamliel the Elder's time. Perhaps he lived a long life. End of quotation. Rashi writes in Ḥullin (32a): 'Yeshavav is a sage's name; so too in Rosh HaShanah' (a scribal error: it should read, 'So too in I Chronicles, chapter 24'; this is Rashi's wording), concerning the priestly watches. Thus Yeshavav is the name of the fourteenth watch. He was one of the ten martyrs killed by the government. They killed him during the recitation of Shema, when he said, 'And they shall make fringes for themselves.' He was fasting, was thrown to dogs, and was neither eulogized nor buried. He was like Moses except for prophecy; fortunate is he! He sat before R. Elazar ben Azaryah (see his entry). In R. Yehoshua's name, Ḥullin, chapter 2, mishnah 4 (32).
